body:
What was the Delhi Sultanate?

The Delhi Sultanate refers to the succession of 5 ruling dynasties that governed from Delhi between 1206 and 1526 CE. Their rulers were known as Sultans. During these 320 years, the Sultanate developed from a group of northern Indian territories into a large political power whose armies reached different parts of the Indian subcontinent.

The Sultanate was not a single, continuously united empire. Its territorial extent, political strength and control over provincial governors changed considerably under different rulers. Some Sultans expanded their territories through conquest, while others concentrated on defending existing possessions or restoring control over rebellious regions.

Delhi before the establishment of the Sultanate

Delhi became an important political and commercial centre during the 12th century. The Tomara Rajputs established Delhi as a capital, and the Chauhans or Chahamanas of Ajmer subsequently gained control of it. Delhi developed as a trading centre under these rulers.

A major turning point occurred in 1192, when Muhammad of Ghor defeated Prithviraj Chauhan in the Second Battle of Tarain. This victory strengthened Ghurid control in northern India and prepared the ground for the subsequent establishment of the Delhi Sultanate.

However, 1192 and 1206 represent different events. The victory at Tarain occurred in 1192, whereas the Delhi Sultanate is conventionally dated from 1206, when Muhammad of Ghor's former military commander Qutbuddin Aibak established independent rule after Ghor's death.

Muhammad of Ghor laid the foundation for Turkish political control through his conquests, but Qutbuddin Aibak is identified as the founder and first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate in 1206.

The 5 ruling dynasties

Five dynasties ruled consecutively during the Sultanate period. Their sequence and approximate periods are central chronological facts.

DynastyPeriodFounder
Mamluk or Slave1206–1290Qutbuddin Aibak
Khalji1290–1320Jalaluddin Khalji
Tughlaq1320–1414Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq
Sayyid1414–1451Khizr Khan
Lodi1451–1526Bahlul Lodi

The Mamluks are also called the Early Turkish Rulers in NCERT chronology tables. The name Slave Dynasty refers to the military-slave background of important early rulers, particularly Aibak and Iltutmish. It does not mean that every ruler remained an enslaved person while governing.

The Khaljis and Tughlaqs subsequently enlarged the political and military reach of Delhi. The Sayyids inherited a much smaller kingdom after the weakening of the Tughlaqs. The Lodis, who were of Afghan origin, formed the last dynasty.

How the Sultanate expanded and contracted

Initial consolidation

During the early 13th century, the Delhi Sultans controlled important fortified settlements and military centres. A garrison town was a fortified settlement occupied by soldiers. Maintaining control over the surrounding countryside was more difficult than holding the town itself.

The land surrounding a town that supplied agricultural produce and other necessities was called its hinterland. The rulers gradually extended their authority over these areas to obtain revenue, protect communication routes and support their armies.

Expansion across northern and southern India

During the later 13th and early 14th centuries, the Sultanate consolidated its position in the northern plains and expanded into regions including Rajasthan, Gujarat and Malwa. Military campaigns subsequently reached the Deccan and southern India.

Expansion occurred through different arrangements. Some conquered territories were placed under governors appointed by Delhi. Other rulers acknowledged the Sultan's superiority and agreed to pay tribute, meaning wealth or payments offered by a subordinate ruler. Such tribute did not necessarily establish permanent, direct administration.

Decline of central control

During the later Tughlaq period, repeated rebellions and the difficulty of governing distant territories weakened Delhi's authority. By the 15th century, important regions such as Gujarat, Bengal, Malwa and Jaunpur had established independent political centres.

The Delhi Sultanate finally ended in 1526, when Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi in the First Battle of Panipat. This marked the beginning of Mughal rule in northern India.

Prelims focus

  • 1206–1526: Conventional period of the Delhi Sultanate.
  • 1192: Muhammad of Ghor defeated Prithviraj Chauhan at the Second Battle of Tarain.
  • 1206: Qutbuddin Aibak established the Delhi Sultanate.
  • Dynastic order: Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi.
  • 1526: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi in the First Battle of Panipat.
  • Trap: Military expeditions and the collection of tribute did not always mean direct administration of the conquered territory.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, Chapter 3, The Delhi Sultans, printed pp. 30–35 and 42, 2020–21 reprint; NCERT, Delhi: 12th to 15th Century, Chapter 3, printed pp. 30–31, 2024–25 reprint, online edition consulted 19 November 2026; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Std 7, Chapter 2, The Delhi Sultanate; IGNOU eGyanKosh, Territorial Expansion, Unit 15, Sections 15.1–15.3, consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: The Delhi Sultanate: Origin, Five Dynasties and Political Expansion

body:
The establishment of Mamluk rule

The Mamluk Dynasty, also known as the Slave Dynasty, was the first dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate. It ruled between 1206 and 1290.

The term Mamluk means a military slave. Important early Turkish commanders had entered military service as enslaved persons and received specialised training. Some subsequently acquired substantial political authority and established their own rule.

The dynasty's principal rulers included Qutbuddin Aibak, Shamsuddin Iltutmish, Raziyya Sultan and Ghiyasuddin Balban. Their reigns illustrate the gradual transformation of the Sultanate from a newly established kingdom into a more organised political power.

Qutbuddin Aibak: Founder of the Delhi Sultanate

Establishment of independent rule in 1206

Qutbuddin Aibak (1206–1210) was a military commander of Muhammad of Ghor. He helped extend Ghurid authority in northern India and established his own rule after Muhammad of Ghor died in 1206.

Aibak is therefore regarded as the founder and first Sultan of the Delhi Sultanate. He worked to preserve the territories established through the earlier Ghurid conquests.

Aibak is traditionally known as Lakh Baksh, meaning a generous giver. He began the construction of the Qutb Minar in Delhi and was associated with the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque. The construction of the Qutb Minar was continued by Iltutmish.

Aibak died in 1210 after an accident while playing chaugan, a game resembling polo, at Lahore.

Shamsuddin Iltutmish: Consolidator of the Sultanate

Strengthening Delhi's political authority

Shamsuddin Iltutmish (1210–1236 in NCERT chronology) succeeded to power following Aibak's death and an intervening succession struggle. Although Aibak established the Sultanate, Iltutmish is often regarded as its effective consolidator.

Iltutmish established Delhi as the principal centre of his government. He strengthened the kingdom against rival Turkish commanders and regional challenges. His reign helped transform a collection of territories into a more stable Sultanate.

He also received formal recognition from the Abbasid Caliph in 1229. This recognition strengthened his political legitimacy, although effective authority in India depended upon his own administration and military power.

The Chahalgani

Iltutmish organised an influential group of Turkish nobles commonly known as the Chahalgani or Turkan-i-Chahalgani, associated with a group of 40 Turkish nobles.

These nobles assisted the ruler in military and administrative affairs. However, their influence created difficulties when succession disputes arose. Powerful nobles could support or oppose particular claimants to the throne.

Coins and administrative consolidation

Iltutmish is credited with establishing an important standardised monetary system, particularly the silver tanka and the copper jital. These became significant denominations in the monetary system of the Delhi Sultanate.

He also relied upon trained military servants and officials for administration. This helped strengthen the Sultan's authority over governors and military commanders.

Raziyya Sultan: The first woman to rule Delhi as Sultan

Raziyya Sultan (1236–1240) was the daughter of Iltutmish. She became the first woman Sultan of Delhi in 1236.

Her accession was exceptional because powerful Turkish nobles generally expected political authority to remain in male hands. Raziyya attempted to exercise independent royal authority rather than remain under the control of influential nobles.

The contemporary chronicler Minhaj-i-Siraj acknowledged her administrative ability but was uncomfortable with female sovereignty. Noble opposition, political rivalries and rebellions ultimately weakened her position. She was removed from power in 1240.

Raziyya was not merely the wife of a ruler or a royal adviser. She occupied the throne and governed as Sultan. Her reign must also be distinguished from that of other medieval women rulers, such as Rudramadevi of the Kakatiya dynasty.

Ghiyasuddin Balban: Strong central authority

Ghiyasuddin Balban (1266–1287) was another major Mamluk ruler. He had exercised considerable political influence before becoming Sultan.

Balban attempted to strengthen the authority of the monarchy and reduce the excessive influence of powerful Turkish nobles. He curtailed the political importance of the Chahalgani and demanded strict obedience to royal authority.

His methods are commonly associated with a policy of blood and iron, referring to the severe measures he used against rebellions and challenges to the throne.

Balban also took measures to defend the northwestern frontier against Mongol attacks. He strengthened military preparedness and attempted to maintain control over regions where local chiefs or governors resisted Delhi's authority.

The changing relationship between the Sultan and the nobles

The experiences of Iltutmish, Raziyya and Balban show why the relationship between the Sultan and powerful nobles was a central political issue.

  • Iltutmish: Strengthened the monarchy partly through the support of influential Turkish nobles.
  • Raziyya: Faced opposition when she attempted to rule independently of powerful nobles.
  • Balban: Attempted to subordinate powerful nobles to a stronger monarchy.

Following Balban's reign, further succession struggles weakened the dynasty. In 1290, the Khaljis replaced the Mamluks as the ruling dynasty of Delhi.

Prelims focus

  • Qutbuddin Aibak: Founder of the Delhi Sultanate in 1206; began construction of the Qutb Minar.
  • Iltutmish: Consolidated the Sultanate, organised the Chahalgani and standardised the tanka and jital coinage.
  • Raziyya Sultan: First woman Sultan of Delhi; ruled from 1236 to 1240.
  • Balban: Strengthened royal authority and acted firmly against rebellions and powerful nobles.
  • 1290: End of the Mamluk Dynasty and beginning of Khalji rule.
  • Trap: Aibak founded the Sultanate, whereas Iltutmish is associated with its effective consolidation.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, Chapter 3, The Delhi Sultans, printed pp. 31–40; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Std 7, Chapter 2, The Delhi Sultanate; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, History, Std 11, Chapter 14, Delhi Sultanate, printed pp. 121–122; IGNOU eGyanKosh, BHIC-107, Unit 9, Land Administration, section on Sultanate coinage, consulted 19 November 2026.]
